what_its_for: Epoetin alfa helps your body make more red blood cells. It is used to treat anemia (low red blood cell count) caused by chronic kidney disease, chemotherapy for cancer, or HIV/AIDS medicines. It may also be used before certain surgeries to reduce the need for blood transfusions.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a vein (intravenous). Your doctor or nurse will teach you how to give yourself the injection at home. Always use a new needle and syringe each time. Inject into your upper arm, thigh, or belly area. Do not shake the vial. Check the liquid before use — it should be clear and colorless. Do not use it if it looks cloudy, has particles, or has changed color.
dosing: Your dose depends on your condition, weight, and how well your body responds to the medicine. Your doctor will start you on a low dose and adjust it based on your blood tests. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to find the right dose for you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, give it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at the same time. Call your doctor or pharmacist if you are unsure what to do.
storage: Store epoetin alfa in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it — throw it away if it has been frozen. Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. Do not shake the vial. Single-dose vials (small bottles) must be thrown away after one use, even if medicine is left inside. Multidose vials can be used more than once but must be used within 21 days of the first use. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Do not drive or use heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it may cause dizziness. Avoid getting pregnant while on this medicine unless directed by your doctor — talk to your doctor about birth control. Do not use this medicine if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure. Avoid starting new medications, vitamins, or supplements without telling your doctor first, as some medicines can interact with epoetin alfa.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: chest pain or tightness, sudden severe headache, confusion, trouble speaking or understanding speech, sudden vision changes, weakness or numbness on one side of your body, pain or swelling in your leg (possible blood clot), shortness of breath, swelling of your face or hands, skin rash or hives, or a very high blood pressure reading. Also call your doctor if you notice your symptoms of anemia (like tiredness or dizziness) are not getting better or are getting worse.
when_it_works: Epoetin alfa does not work overnight. It usually takes 2 to 6 weeks before your red blood cell count begins to rise and you start feeling less tired. Your doctor will check your blood regularly to see how well the medicine is working. Be patient and keep taking it as directed even if you do not feel a difference right away.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The risks and benefits need to be carefully discussed with your doctor. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially high blood pressure and blood clots — your doctor will monitor you closely. Children: This medicine can be used in children, but dosing is carefully adjusted by weight. Kidney disease patients: Your doctor will monitor your blood pressure and blood counts very carefully, as this medicine can raise blood pressure. Cancer patients: This medicine should only be used during chemotherapy and at the lowest dose needed — it should be stopped when your chemotherapy is finished.
